findings.where: Screen 7 (Slide the frequency), end of the demonstration; lesson JSON whatAmILookingAt
findings.what: The demonstration ends at 0 Hz, so its settled frame shows the ammeter at 3.33 A, V_R at 20 V and a flat triangle directly above the real-coil rows that read 'AC meters at 50 Hz: Z = 20 V ÷ 2 A = 10 Ω'. The picture contradicts the working under it. whatAmILookingAt also promises that the resistor and coil 'slide together into one real coil' back at 50 Hz, which the body never draws. Add a third morph segment from 0 back to 50 Hz before tl.real, and draw the dashed one-body outline as the coil8 card does, or cut that sentence from the JSON.
'Each arrow is as long as its meter's rms reading' is untrue on screens 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 12, where the arrows are in ohms. Say 'each arrow is as long as its reading, in volts or ohms'.

findings.where: Lead line above the stepper (all screens)
findings.what: The lead repeats step 1's first sentence word for word, so the opening screen says it twice in a row. It also stays on every screen and still names the 25.5 mH coil bench on screens 4, 6, 8, 9 and 11, where the circuit is different. Drop it or make it generic.

findings.where: Screen 6 (On the mains); practice worked example
findings.what: Screen 6 is Complex numbers lesson 8's sum again: a 3-4-5 impedance on 230 V with part voltages of 138 V and 184 V, the very numbers that lesson used. That goes against the brief's 'never the same sums again' for this lesson. The worked example then reuses the same 30 Ω, 40 Ω, 230 V and 4.6 A circuit. Pitch screen 6 at meters, for example three meter readings in, R and X_L out.

findings.where: Screens 1, 6 and 11 and the worked example
findings.what: Four of the seven triangles are 3-4-5 (6-8-10, 30-40-50 twice in ohms, 30-40-50 in volts), so 53.13° keeps coming back and could read as typical. Give screen 11 or the worked example a different shape.
The slider snaps to 60 Hz, where the rows show 1.77 A at 58.0°, the exact answer to screen 12's mixed puzzle, five screens before it is asked. Take 60 out of the snap points.

The right answer is the only option that names all four figures and is visibly the longest, so it can be picked by its shape. Make the wrong options full namings too, for example 'Resistance 6 Ω, reactances 10 Ω, impedance 8 Ω'.

'Swap in a capacitor and that run turns the other way, which no tape would show' is not a break: a run round the other corner fits the analogy exactly, and the meters do not show direction either. Replace it with a true break: the meter readings change with frequency, and a cable's length does not.

The iron-loss caveat (iron loss acts as extra resistance an ohmmeter cannot see, so the inductance comes out a little high) has no source in the notes. The direction checks out by the lesson's own rule (a larger true R leaves a smaller X), so label it as reasoning from the rule, or cite it.
The key entry 'closing side, swung flat' and the swing dot appear abruptly instead of fading in, because keyRows is given a = swOn, which is only 0 or 1. Fade both with arr(tl.sw[0]).

At 360 px the swatches for 'current, the reference' (grey dash 4 4) and 'the 50 Hz triangle' (grey dash 3 3) look the same. Make the ghost swatch a short closed triangle, or give the two lines clearly different dashes.

The only control is the frequency, and only on screens 7 and 9. The brief's drags of R and L are not built, so Dan never moves R and sees φ change at a fixed frequency. An R slider on screen 7 would let him test 'only the reactance side depends on frequency'.

The two frequency sweeps are drawn in different units: ohms with R fixed on screen 7, and volts with the 20 V side fixed on screen 9. The same experiment therefore looks different, and screen 9's text quotes X_C in ohms while the drawn side is V_C in volts. Add one line on screen 9 saying the triangle is in volts here, with the supply side fixed at 20 V.
Five sentences carry nine numbers before 'Slide the frequency yourself'. Keep the cause (X_L grows with f, R does not) and let the rows carry the figures.
